How it works

Each order is processed on exactly one machine that can handle it. The processing time depends on the machine. Every order should finish by its due date; when that is impossible, every order is still assigned and the total lateness is minimized first. Then the selected objective is minimized:

  • Total processing time: the sum of the processing times on the chosen machines. Putting every order on its fastest machine gives the lower bound, but usually some orders then miss their due dates.
  • Makespan: the time at which the last order finishes. Among the schedules with the same makespan, the one with the smallest total processing time is chosen.

QUBO++ processes the orders of each machine in due-date order, which is always the best way to meet the due dates, so only the assignment has to be decided (you can still reorder them by hand). With a binary variable y[j][m] that is 1 when order j is processed on machine m, order j finishes on machine m at C[j][m] = Σi ≤ j p[i][m]·y[i][m], where i ≤ j runs over the orders with due dates no later than that of j, and machine m is busy for L[m] = Σj p[j][m]·y[j][m].

  • Each order on exactly one machine: cons(Σm y[j][m] == 1)
  • Lateness of order j on machine m: relu(C[j][m] − d[j] − H[j][m]·(1 − y[j][m])). H[j][m] is the largest possible lateness, so the term is 0 when the order is not on machine m.
  • Makespan: an integer variable z with the terms V·z + (V + 1)·Σm relu(L[m] − z). Each minute of z below the longest machine costs more than it saves, so z becomes the makespan.
  • Objective: minimize W·(total lateness) + V·z + Σ p[j][m]·y[j][m] (V = 0 and no z for the total processing time). The weights make 5 minutes of lateness cost more than any change in the rest, and 5 minutes of makespan more than any change in the total processing time, so the due dates come first.

QUBO++ handles cons(), relu() and integer variables directly, so the model has only the assignment variables and z: no slack variables are needed. The search stops early when it reaches the lower bound, which proves optimality.
